subject.name: Spring Boot
subject.description: Prepare for Spring Boot interviews, from application fundamentals and dependency injection to REST APIs, persistence, security, testing, observability, and production architecture.

topics.name: Spring Boot Fundamentals
topics.description: Spring Boot application structure, starters, embedded servers, and application lifecycle.

topics.name: Auto-Configuration & Starters
topics.description: Conditional configuration, starter dependencies, and understanding Spring Boot's conventions.

topics.name: Dependency Injection & Configuration
topics.description: Beans, scopes, configuration properties, profiles, and application configuration.

topics.name: REST APIs & Web Layer
topics.description: Spring MVC controllers, request mapping, serialization, and HTTP semantics.

topics.name: Validation & Exception Handling
topics.description: Bean Validation, request validation, exception mapping, and API error design.

topics.name: Spring Data JPA & Persistence
topics.description: Repositories, entity mapping, fetching, pagination, and persistence context behavior.

topics.name: Transactions & Data Consistency
topics.description: Transaction boundaries, propagation, isolation, rollback rules, and consistency.

topics.name: Spring Security
topics.description: Authentication, authorization, filter chains, OAuth2/JWT concepts, and security configuration.

topics.name: Testing Spring Boot Applications
topics.description: Unit tests, integration tests, MockMvc, test slices, and test database strategies.

topics.name: Actuator, Observability & Operations
topics.description: Health checks, metrics, logging, tracing, readiness, and production operations.

topics.name: Microservices & Messaging
topics.description: Service communication, resilience, event-driven patterns, and messaging integration.

topics.name: Performance & Production Design
topics.description: Application startup, connection pools, caching, scalability, and production readiness.

questions.question: What is Spring Boot Actuator primarily used for?

options.text: Exposing operational endpoints and application information such as health and metrics
Generating Java source code
Replacing the logging framework
Creating database entities

questions.explanation: Actuator provides production-oriented features such as health, metrics, environment information, and application diagnostics. Exposed endpoints must be configured and secured carefully.

questions.question: What does the Actuator health endpoint generally report?

options.text: The application's health status and, when configured, health details from contributing components
A complete list of all source code files
The full contents of every database table
The application's Git history

questions.explanation: The health endpoint aggregates `HealthIndicator` contributions and reports an overall status. Details may be restricted based on configuration and authorization.

questions.question: What is the difference between liveness and readiness probes?

options.text: Liveness indicates whether the process should be restarted; readiness indicates whether it should receive traffic
Liveness checks database schema; readiness checks source control
They are identical signals
Readiness determines whether the JVM can start

questions.explanation: Liveness helps an orchestrator decide whether to restart a stuck or unhealthy process. Readiness indicates whether the instance should receive traffic, for example while dependencies or startup initialization are incomplete.

questions.question: Which Micrometer concept is commonly used to instrument application metrics?

options.text: MeterRegistry
EntityManagerFactory
DispatcherServletMapping
BeanDefinitionReader

questions.explanation: Micrometer provides a vendor-neutral metrics facade. A `MeterRegistry` records counters, timers, gauges, and other meters and can publish them to supported monitoring systems.

questions.question: Why should high-cardinality values such as user IDs generally not be used as metric tags?

options.text: They can create an unbounded number of time series and increase monitoring-system cost and resource use
They prevent metrics from being exported over HTTP
They make counters decrement automatically
They disable log correlation

questions.explanation: Metric labels should have bounded cardinality. Per-user or per-request identifiers can create enormous numbers of time series; put high-cardinality identifiers in logs or traces instead.

questions.question: What is distributed tracing intended to help diagnose?

options.text: The path and timing of a request as it crosses multiple services
The exact contents of a database backup
The number of Java source files
The CSS rendering time of a browser

questions.explanation: Distributed tracing correlates spans across service boundaries, helping identify latency, dependency calls, and failures in a distributed request flow.

questions.question: What is a useful principle when exposing Actuator endpoints in production?

options.text: Expose only required endpoints and protect sensitive operational information with appropriate access controls
Expose every endpoint publicly for easier debugging
Disable authentication on management endpoints
Return environment variables to all callers

questions.explanation: Operational endpoints can reveal configuration, environment, mappings, or other sensitive details. Minimize exposure, isolate management traffic where appropriate, and apply strong authorization.

questions.question: What is the purpose of structured logging?

options.text: To emit logs with consistent fields that can be searched, filtered, and correlated by log platforms
To compress all logs into binary files
To prevent exceptions from being logged
To replace metrics and traces completely

questions.explanation: Structured logs use fields such as timestamp, severity, service, trace ID, and event attributes. They improve querying and correlation compared with unstructured text alone.

questions.question: Why should secrets generally not be stored in committed `application.yml` files?

options.text: They can be exposed through source control history, builds, and developer access; use a managed secret mechanism instead
YAML cannot represent strings securely
Spring Boot cannot read encrypted values
Secrets make auto-configuration fail

questions.explanation: Committed secrets are difficult to contain even after deletion because they may remain in repository history and copies. Use a secret manager or secure deployment-time injection and rotate exposed credentials.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a custom `HealthIndicator`?

options.text: To contribute application-specific health information to the Actuator health system
To define a custom HTTP serializer
To register a JPA entity listener
To modify Java garbage collection

questions.explanation: A custom `HealthIndicator` can report the health of an application-specific dependency or capability. Health checks should be bounded and designed not to overload dependencies.

questions.question: What does Spring Boot auto-configuration primarily do?

options.text: Automatically writes application business logic
Configures beans based on classpath contents, existing beans, and configuration properties
Creates a new database for every application
Disables explicit configuration

questions.explanation: Auto-configuration contributes configuration when its conditions match. It commonly checks available classes, properties, and whether an application has already supplied a bean. Developers can override defaults by defining their own configuration.

questions.question: What is a Spring Boot starter?

options.text: A curated dependency descriptor that brings in a useful set of related dependencies
A Java class that starts every bean manually
A replacement for the Spring container
A production deployment server

questions.explanation: Starters simplify dependency management by grouping commonly used libraries for a capability, such as web, validation, data JPA, or security.

questions.question: Which annotation is commonly used to enable a configuration class only when a class is present on the classpath?

options.text: @ConditionalOnClass
@Primary
@Order
@Lazy

questions.explanation: `@ConditionalOnClass` is one of Boot's condition annotations. It allows configuration to match only when specified classes are available, helping auto-configuration adapt to the application's dependencies.

questions.question: What does `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` typically allow an auto-configuration to do?

options.text: Create a default bean only when the application has not already provided a matching bean
Create a bean only when a database row is missing
Disable all user-defined beans
Force two beans to have the same name

questions.explanation: It backs off when a matching bean already exists, allowing application-specific beans to replace Boot defaults.

questions.question: How can a developer inspect which auto-configurations matched or did not match during startup?

options.text: Use the condition evaluation report, for example by enabling the debug startup report
Read the JVM heap dump only
Enable SQL logging only
Inspect the browser developer console

questions.explanation: Boot can print a condition evaluation report when debug mode is enabled. Actuator's conditions endpoint may also expose condition information when appropriately configured and secured.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `@ConditionalOnProperty`?

options.text: To apply configuration when a specified property has a matching value or is present, depending on its settings
To validate every HTTP request body
To map a Java field to a database column
To select a transaction isolation level

questions.explanation: `@ConditionalOnProperty` lets configuration be enabled or disabled through environment properties, often using a feature flag such as `feature.audit.enabled=true`.

questions.question: What is the recommended modern mechanism for registering custom auto-configuration in a Spring Boot library?

options.text: List the auto-configuration class in `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`
Add it only to `web.xml`
Put it in the root package and rely on component scanning by every consumer
Register it in the JVM manifest

questions.explanation: Modern Spring Boot versions use the `AutoConfiguration.imports` resource to list auto-configuration classes. Older Boot versions used `spring.factories` for this purpose.

questions.question: Why should auto-configuration classes generally avoid broad component scanning?

options.text: Broad scanning can unexpectedly register application components from packages that the library does not own
Component scanning prevents conditional annotations from working
It makes all beans prototype scoped
It disables configuration properties

questions.explanation: Library auto-configuration should be explicit and narrowly scoped. Broad scanning can cause bean collisions and surprising side effects in consuming applications.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `@AutoConfiguration` in recent Spring Boot versions?

options.text: It marks a class as an auto-configuration candidate
It marks a controller as reactive
It enables database migrations
It turns a class into a test fixture

questions.explanation: `@AutoConfiguration` is a specialized configuration annotation intended for Boot auto-configuration classes. It communicates the class's role and supports ordering metadata.

questions.question: What is a practical reason to exclude a specific auto-configuration?

options.text: The application intentionally supplies an alternative or does not want that integration configured
The application needs to increase HTTP request throughput automatically
The application wants to skip Java compilation
The application wants to remove all Spring beans

questions.explanation: Exclusions are useful when a default integration is unwanted or conflicts with an intentional alternative. They should be targeted rather than used as a substitute for understanding configuration conditions.

questions.question: Which injection style is generally recommended for required dependencies in Spring components?

options.text: Field injection
Constructor injection
Static injection
Lookup through a global application context

questions.explanation: Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit, supports immutable fields, simplifies unit testing, and avoids partially initialized objects. A single constructor does not usually need `@Autowired`.

questions.question: What does `@Component` do?

options.text: Marks a class as a candidate for component scanning and bean registration
Starts an HTTP server
Creates a database table
Enables transaction management by itself

questions.explanation: `@Component` is a stereotype annotation. Spring can discover it through component scanning and register an instance as a bean.

questions.question: When should `@ConfigurationProperties` be preferred over many individual `@Value` fields?

options.text: When binding a group of related configuration properties into a typed object
Only when injecting a single constant
When mapping request parameters to a controller
When declaring JPA relationships

questions.explanation: `@ConfigurationProperties` provides structured, type-safe binding for related settings, supports validation, and is easier to organize and test than many unrelated `@Value` expressions.

questions.question: What is the default scope of a Spring bean?

options.text: Prototype
Request
Singleton
Session

questions.explanation: Singleton is the default: one bean instance per bean definition per Spring application context. It does not mean one instance per JVM across all contexts.

questions.question: What happens when two beans of the same type are candidates for a single injection point and no qualifier or primary bean resolves the ambiguity?

options.text: Spring normally reports a NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
Spring silently injects both into every field
Spring always chooses the bean created first
The application automatically changes both beans to prototype scope

questions.explanation: An ambiguous single-valued dependency normally causes a startup failure. Resolve it with `@Primary`, `@Qualifier`, or a more specific injection design.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Spring profiles?

options.text: To activate environment-specific bean definitions and configuration
To encrypt all properties automatically
To create a separate JVM for each environment
To define REST API versions

questions.explanation: Profiles allow configuration and beans to be selected for environments such as local, test, staging, and production. Profile activation can come from properties, environment variables, or command-line arguments.

questions.question: What is a potential problem when injecting a prototype-scoped bean directly into a singleton bean?

options.text: The singleton receives one prototype instance at its own creation time rather than a fresh instance on every use
The singleton is converted into a prototype
Spring creates a new singleton for each request
The application context cannot start

questions.explanation: Direct injection resolves the prototype dependency when the singleton is created. If a fresh instance is needed for each operation, use a provider such as `ObjectProvider`, a scoped proxy, or another lookup mechanism.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `@DependsOn`?

options.text: To declare that one bean should be initialized before another bean
To inject a list of all beans
To create a circular dependency automatically
To define a transaction boundary

questions.explanation: `@DependsOn` expresses initialization ordering between named beans. It is not a general replacement for constructor dependencies, which already express a natural dependency relationship.

questions.question: Why can circular constructor dependencies cause application startup to fail?

options.text: Neither object can be constructed without the other being available first
Constructor injection disables component scanning
Spring cannot create more than one bean at a time
All singleton beans must be immutable

questions.explanation: A constructor cycle such as A requiring B and B requiring A prevents either constructor from completing. Refactor responsibilities or introduce an appropriate indirection rather than relying on circular references.

questions.question: What does `@Value("${service.timeout}")` do?

options.text: Injects a property value resolved from the Spring Environment
Creates a property named service.timeout in the database
Validates an incoming HTTP header
Loads a profile-specific class

questions.explanation: `@Value` resolves a property placeholder or expression and injects the resulting value. For groups of related settings, `@ConfigurationProperties` is often more maintainable.

questions.question: What is the primary goal of Spring Boot?

options.text: To eliminate the need for the Spring Framework
To simplify the creation of production-ready Spring applications with opinionated defaults
To replace Java with a configuration language
To provide only an embedded database

questions.explanation: Spring Boot builds on the Spring Framework. It reduces setup and configuration through auto-configuration, starter dependencies, embedded servers, and operational features. It does not replace Spring or require a particular database.

questions.question: Which annotation is commonly used on the main class of a Spring Boot application?

options.text: @EnableWebMvc
@SpringBootApplication
@ConfigurationProperties
@ComponentScan only

questions.explanation: `@SpringBootApplication` combines `@SpringBootConfiguration`, `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, and `@ComponentScan`. It is the conventional entry-point annotation for a Boot application.

questions.question: What does `SpringApplication.run(MyApplication.class, args)` do?

options.text: Compiles all Java source files
Creates and refreshes the Spring application context and starts the application
Runs only the unit tests
Generates database schema files

questions.explanation: `SpringApplication.run` bootstraps the application: it prepares the environment, creates the appropriate application context, registers beans, refreshes the context, and starts the embedded web server when applicable.

questions.question: Which embedded servlet container is commonly used by default by the standard Spring Boot web starter?

options.text: Tomcat
WebLogic
IBM WebSphere
IIS

questions.explanation: `spring-boot-starter-web` traditionally brings embedded Tomcat by default. Jetty or Undertow can be used by replacing the relevant server dependency. The exact default can depend on the Boot generation and selected starter.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of an executable Spring Boot JAR?

options.text: It contains a complete operating system
It packages the application and its dependencies so it can be launched with `java -jar`
It removes the JVM requirement
It guarantees that the application has no external configuration

questions.explanation: An executable Boot JAR packages application classes and dependencies in a Boot-compatible layout and includes a launcher. A compatible Java runtime is still required, and external configuration or infrastructure may still be needed.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `SpringApplicationBuilder`?

options.text: To build SQL queries
To configure and build Spring applications or application contexts programmatically
To generate REST controllers
To replace Maven

questions.explanation: `SpringApplicationBuilder` provides a fluent API for configuring an application, including profiles, properties, parent/child contexts, and application sources.

questions.question: Which file is a conventional location for externalized Spring Boot configuration?

options.text: application.properties or application.yml
pom.xml only
MANIFEST.MF only
settings.gradle only

questions.explanation: Boot loads configuration from multiple locations and formats. `application.properties` and `application.yml` are conventional application configuration files; command-line arguments, environment variables, and external files can override values according to property-source precedence.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `spring-boot-starter-parent` Maven parent?

options.text: It provides dependency and plugin management defaults for Boot projects
It replaces the Java compiler
It runs the application in Kubernetes
It stores application secrets

questions.explanation: The starter parent provides managed dependency versions, plugin management, and useful Maven defaults. Projects can instead import the Spring Boot dependency BOM and manage their own parent.

questions.question: What is the most accurate statement about Spring Boot's embedded server?

options.text: It is mandatory for every Spring Boot application
It is started for web application types that use an embedded web server; non-web applications need not start one
It runs in a separate operating system process
It replaces the application context

questions.explanation: Boot supports servlet, reactive, and non-web application types. A servlet or reactive web application commonly starts an embedded server; a command-line or other non-web application does not need one.

questions.question: What is the role of `ApplicationRunner`?

options.text: To execute application logic after the application context has been created and startup is nearly complete
To run before the JVM starts
To intercept every HTTP request
To replace bean initialization callbacks

questions.explanation: `ApplicationRunner` is called with parsed application arguments after the application context has been refreshed. It is useful for startup tasks that need initialized Spring beans. `CommandLineRunner` serves a similar purpose with raw string arguments.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a Spring Data JPA repository interface?

options.text: To provide a repository abstraction for common persistence operations with generated implementations
To replace the relational database
To render HTML templates
To configure HTTP security

questions.explanation: Spring Data JPA creates repository implementations for interfaces such as `JpaRepository`, providing CRUD, pagination, sorting, and query derivation capabilities.

questions.question: Which annotation marks a class as a JPA entity?

options.text: @Entity
@Component
@RestController
@Configuration

questions.explanation: `@Entity` marks a class as a persistent entity managed by the JPA provider. It normally requires an identifier annotated with `@Id`.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `@ManyToOne` in JPA?

options.text: It maps a many-to-one association from one entity to another
It declares a one-to-one relationship
It marks a field as a primary key
It enables optimistic locking

questions.explanation: `@ManyToOne` models an association where many source entities can reference one target entity, commonly represented by a foreign key on the source table.

questions.question: What is the N+1 query problem?

options.text: One query loads a collection of parent records, then an additional query is issued for each parent to load related data
A query returns exactly N plus one rows
The database creates N indexes automatically
A transaction is retried N+1 times

questions.explanation: The N+1 problem often occurs when lazy associations are accessed in a loop. It can be addressed with fetch joins, entity graphs, projections, or deliberate batch fetching, depending on the use case.

questions.question: What does `Pageable` enable in Spring Data repositories?

options.text: Pagination and sorting parameters for repository queries
Automatic database sharding
Distributed transactions
JSON request validation

questions.explanation: `Pageable` carries page number, page size, and sorting information. Repository methods can use it to retrieve a page and metadata about the result set.

questions.question: What is the difference between `findByEmail` and `findByEmailIgnoreCase` in a derived Spring Data query?

options.text: The latter requests case-insensitive matching for the email property
The latter always performs a full table scan
The former returns a stream and the latter a list
There is no difference

questions.explanation: Spring Data parses method names into query predicates. `IgnoreCase` requests case-insensitive comparison for supported property types and query strategies.

questions.question: What is a common reason for `LazyInitializationException`?

options.text: Accessing an uninitialized lazy association after the persistence context has been closed
Using an eager association inside a transaction
Calling a repository method from a service
Declaring a primary key

questions.explanation: A lazy proxy needs an active persistence context to initialize. Accessing it after the session/entity manager is closed can fail. Design fetch plans and transaction boundaries deliberately rather than making every relationship eager.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `@Version` on a JPA entity field?

options.text: To support optimistic locking by detecting conflicting updates
To store the application version
To enable pessimistic database locks on every query
To define a composite primary key

questions.explanation: A version attribute is checked and incremented during updates. If another transaction has changed the row, the provider can detect the conflict and raise an optimistic locking exception.

questions.question: What is the main difference between `save` and `saveAndFlush` in Spring Data JPA?

options.text: `saveAndFlush` requests synchronization of pending persistence-context changes with the database immediately; `save` does not guarantee an immediate flush
`save` commits the transaction; `saveAndFlush` never writes to the database
`saveAndFlush` always creates a new transaction
There is no difference in all circumstances

questions.explanation: `save` persists or merges an entity but the SQL may be deferred until flush or commit. `saveAndFlush` explicitly flushes the persistence context, but it does not itself guarantee transaction commit.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `@EntityGraph` in Spring Data JPA?

options.text: To specify associations to fetch for a query without hard-coding a fetch join into the query text
To draw an entity relationship diagram at runtime
To generate database migration scripts
To enable second-level cache automatically

questions.explanation: `@EntityGraph` defines a fetch plan for an entity query, allowing selected associations to be loaded as part of that operation. It helps address use-case-specific fetching needs.

questions.question: Why should microservices generally avoid sharing the same database schema as a single tightly coupled data model?

options.text: Shared schemas create deployment and ownership coupling between services
A relational database cannot serve multiple services
Microservices cannot use SQL
Sharing a schema automatically provides event sourcing

questions.explanation: Independent service ownership of data reduces coupling and allows services to evolve their persistence models. Cross-service data needs are commonly handled through APIs, events, or read models.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a circuit breaker in service-to-service communication?

options.text: Stop repeated calls to a failing dependency temporarily and allow recovery checks
Encrypt messages between services
Guarantee exactly-once delivery
Replace all retry logic with infinite retries

questions.explanation: A circuit breaker transitions between closed, open, and half-open states based on failures. It can prevent cascading failures by failing fast while a dependency is unhealthy.

questions.question: What is the main risk of using unbounded retries for a failing downstream service?

options.text: Retries can amplify load and worsen an outage
Retries guarantee lower latency
Retries remove the need for timeouts
Retries make non-idempotent operations safe

questions.explanation: Retry storms can overload an already unhealthy dependency. Use bounded retries, backoff, jitter, timeouts, and retry only failures that are plausibly transient and safe to repeat.

questions.question: What does idempotency mean for an API operation?

options.text: Repeating the same request has the same intended effect as performing it once
The request can only be sent once
The request never changes server state
The response must always be identical byte-for-byte

questions.explanation: An idempotent operation can be repeated without multiplying its intended effect. This is important for safe retries; an idempotency key is often used for operations such as payment creation.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a message broker such as Kafka or RabbitMQ in an event-driven system?

options.text: To decouple producers and consumers and support asynchronous message delivery
To replace every service's database
To compile Java classes
To enforce HTTP request validation

questions.explanation: A broker buffers and routes messages, allowing producers and consumers to operate independently in time and scale. Delivery semantics, ordering, retention, and acknowledgments depend on the broker and configuration.

questions.question: Why should message consumers commonly be designed to handle duplicate delivery?

options.text: Many broker and failure scenarios can cause a message to be delivered more than once
All brokers guarantee duplicate delivery
Consumers cannot acknowledge messages
Duplicate messages always have different IDs

questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery and retry/rebalance scenarios can produce duplicates. Consumers should use idempotent processing, deduplication, or transactional techniques appropriate to the system.

questions.question: What is the Saga pattern used for?

options.text: Coordinating a business transaction across multiple services through local transactions and compensating actions
Running one ACID transaction across every database automatically
Replacing service discovery
Compressing events before publication

questions.explanation: A saga decomposes a distributed business process into local transactions. If a later step fails, compensating actions can semantically undo earlier steps; this is not equivalent to a single global ACID transaction.

questions.question: What is service discovery used for in a dynamic microservice environment?

options.text: Finding the current network locations of service instances
Discovering Java annotations at compile time
Finding database indexes
Generating OAuth access tokens

questions.explanation: Service discovery provides a way to resolve logical service names to current instances as they scale, restart, or move.

questions.question: Why is distributed tracing context propagated across asynchronous message boundaries?

options.text: So spans from producer and consumer work can be correlated into the same end-to-end trace
So the broker can execute Java code
So message payloads become encrypted automatically
So the consumer can skip authentication

questions.explanation: Propagating trace context in message headers allows observability systems to connect producer and consumer spans, even when processing is asynchronous.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of an API gateway?

options.text: Provide a managed entry point for routing and cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, rate limiting, and request policies
Replace all internal service boundaries
Store every service's domain entities
Guarantee that downstream services never fail

questions.explanation: An API gateway can centralize edge concerns and route requests to backend services. Business authorization and domain rules should still be enforced by the services that own the resources.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a database connection pool such as HikariCP?

options.text: Reuse a bounded set of database connections instead of opening a new connection for every operation
Cache every query result permanently
Replace database transactions
Create one connection per application user

questions.explanation: A connection pool amortizes connection setup cost and limits concurrent database connections. Pool sizing should reflect database capacity and application concurrency rather than simply being made as large as possible.

questions.question: What is a common risk of setting an excessively large JDBC connection pool?

options.text: It can overwhelm the database with too many concurrent connections and increase contention
It guarantees lower database CPU usage
It eliminates query latency
It makes transactions serializable

questions.explanation: More connections do not necessarily increase throughput. A pool larger than the database can efficiently serve may increase context switching, contention, and resource pressure.

questions.question: What is the purpose of caching frequently read, relatively stable data?

options.text: Reduce repeated expensive computation or data retrieval, while introducing freshness and invalidation considerations
Guarantee that data is always current
Eliminate the need for a database
Make every write operation faster

questions.explanation: Caching can reduce latency and backend load. It introduces trade-offs involving TTL, invalidation, consistency, memory use, and cache stampedes.

questions.question: What is a cache stampede?

options.text: Many requests simultaneously attempt to recompute or reload the same expired cache entry
A cache stores too few bytes per entry
A cache key contains a timestamp
A cache returns a value from memory

questions.explanation: When a popular key expires, concurrent misses can overwhelm the backing store. Techniques include request coalescing, locking, stale-while-revalidate, jittered TTLs, and refresh-ahead.

questions.question: Why should outbound HTTP calls from a Spring Boot service have explicit timeouts?

options.text: Without timeouts, requests may wait too long and consume application threads or resources
Timeouts disable TLS
Timeouts guarantee that the remote service responds faster
The JVM applies the same safe timeout to every client automatically

questions.explanation: Explicit connect and response/read timeouts bound resource occupancy and failure detection. The exact settings depend on the HTTP client and the operation's latency budget.

questions.question: What is bulkheading in a service architecture?

options.text: Isolating resources or workloads so failure or saturation in one area does not consume all capacity
Combining every service into one process
Encrypting all network traffic
Increasing every thread pool without limits

questions.explanation: Bulkheads isolate thread pools, connection pools, or concurrency limits by dependency or workload. This reduces the chance that one slow dependency exhausts all resources.

questions.question: Why is pagination important for endpoints that return large collections?

options.text: It bounds response size and database work per request and supports predictable client consumption
It guarantees that every page is read from the cache
It removes the need for indexes
It ensures results never change between pages

questions.explanation: Pagination limits payload and query size. Stable ordering is important; for large or frequently changing datasets, cursor/keyset pagination can be more reliable than offset pagination.

questions.question: What is a benefit of graceful shutdown in a Spring Boot service?

options.text: It allows the application to stop accepting new work and gives in-flight requests or tasks a chance to complete within configured limits
It guarantees zero downtime without orchestration
It forces every database transaction to commit
It prevents all JVM crashes

questions.explanation: Graceful shutdown helps avoid dropping in-flight work during deployments or restarts. It should be combined with readiness handling, bounded shutdown time, and orchestrator termination settings.

questions.question: What is a good first step when a production endpoint has unexpectedly high latency?

options.text: Use metrics, traces, and logs to identify whether time is spent in the application, database, or downstream dependencies
Increase every timeout immediately
Add more application instances without measuring
Disable authentication to reduce overhead

questions.explanation: Start with evidence: inspect latency percentiles, trace spans, error rates, resource saturation, and database behavior. Then target the measured bottleneck and verify the change.

questions.question: Why should a Spring Boot application avoid doing lengthy blocking work on request-handling threads without capacity planning?

options.text: It can exhaust the request thread pool, increasing queueing and causing cascading latency
Blocking work is always executed on a separate thread automatically
It prevents transaction management from working
It makes HTTP responses non-deterministic by definition

questions.explanation: Servlet request threads are finite. Slow downstream calls or long-running work can occupy them and reduce the service's ability to handle new requests. Use bounded concurrency, timeouts, async processing where appropriate, and capacity planning.

questions.question: Which annotation is commonly used to define a REST controller whose return values are written to the HTTP response body?

options.text: @ControllerAdvice
@RestController
@Repository
@Configuration

questions.explanation: `@RestController` combines `@Controller` and `@ResponseBody`, so handler return values are serialized into the response body by message converters.

questions.question: Which annotation binds a path segment such as `/orders/{id}` to a controller method parameter?

options.text: @RequestBody
@PathVariable
@RequestHeader
@ModelAttribute

questions.explanation: `@PathVariable` binds a URI template variable to a method parameter. `@RequestParam` is used for query parameters.

questions.question: Which annotation binds JSON from an HTTP request body to a Java object?

options.text: @RequestBody
@RequestParam
@CookieValue
@ResponseStatus

questions.explanation: `@RequestBody` asks an HTTP message converter, commonly Jackson for JSON, to deserialize the request body into the declared Java type.

questions.question: Which HTTP status code is most appropriate when a resource is successfully created?

options.text: 200 OK in every case
201 Created
204 No Content
302 Found

questions.explanation: `201 Created` indicates that the request created a resource. The response may include a `Location` header identifying the new resource. A `200` can also be valid for some API designs, but 201 is the conventional creation status.

questions.question: What is the typical purpose of `ResponseEntity<T>` in a controller?

options.text: To control the response body, status code, and headers
To open a database transaction
To define a JPA entity
To create a scheduled task

questions.explanation: `ResponseEntity` gives a controller explicit control over the HTTP response status, headers, and body.

questions.question: Which annotation maps HTTP GET requests to a controller method?

options.text: @GetMapping
@PostMapping
@PatchMapping
@DeleteMapping

questions.explanation: `@GetMapping` is a composed shortcut for `@RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET)`. Similar shortcuts exist for POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE.

questions.question: What is the main difference between PUT and PATCH in typical REST semantics?

options.text: PUT generally replaces the target representation; PATCH applies a partial modification
PUT is always read-only; PATCH always creates a resource
PUT is for query parameters; PATCH is for headers
There is no semantic difference

questions.explanation: PUT conventionally replaces the resource representation and is idempotent. PATCH applies a set of partial modifications; its exact semantics depend on the patch format and API contract.

questions.question: Why should a REST controller usually return DTOs rather than exposing JPA entities directly?

options.text: DTOs decouple the API contract from persistence, limit data exposure, and avoid serialization issues with entity graphs
DTOs automatically make every endpoint asynchronous
JPA entities cannot be serialized under any circumstances
DTOs eliminate the need for validation

questions.explanation: Returning entities can expose internal fields, create accidental API coupling, trigger lazy-loading queries, or cause recursion in bidirectional relationships. DTOs provide an explicit API boundary.

questions.question: What is a common risk of performing blocking JPA calls on a reactive WebFlux event-loop thread?

options.text: It can block event-loop threads and reduce the scalability of the reactive request pipeline
It automatically converts JPA to R2DBC
It improves backpressure handling
It causes every transaction to become distributed

questions.explanation: Traditional JPA is blocking. Mixing it directly into reactive event-loop processing can block scarce event-loop threads. Use a blocking MVC stack for blocking persistence or isolate blocking work appropriately; use reactive data access for an end-to-end reactive design.

questions.question: Which annotation can be used to set a fixed HTTP response status on a controller method or exception class?

options.text: @ResponseStatus
@Transactional
@Entity
@Profile

questions.explanation: `@ResponseStatus` declares the HTTP status associated with a handler method or exception. For more dynamic responses, use `ResponseEntity` or exception handlers.

questions.question: What is the distinction between authentication and authorization?

options.text: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines what an identity is allowed to do
Authentication assigns roles; authorization hashes passwords
They are interchangeable terms
Authorization happens only in the database

questions.explanation: Authentication verifies who the caller is. Authorization evaluates whether that authenticated principal may access a resource or perform an action.

questions.question: In modern Spring Security configuration, how is the HTTP security filter chain commonly customized?

options.text: By declaring a `SecurityFilterChain` bean and configuring `HttpSecurity`
By extending `WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter` in all current versions
By adding rules to `application.yml` only
By annotating every entity with `@Secured`

questions.explanation: Modern Spring Security configuration commonly exposes a `SecurityFilterChain` bean. `WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter` was deprecated and removed from current configuration approaches.

questions.question: What is the role of `PasswordEncoder` in Spring Security?

options.text: To hash passwords securely for storage and verify submitted passwords against stored hashes
To encrypt passwords reversibly so they can be displayed
To generate JWT signing keys
To validate SQL statements

questions.explanation: `PasswordEncoder` provides password hashing and matching. A delegating encoder can support versioned formats; passwords should not be stored in plaintext or reversibly encrypted.

questions.question: What is CSRF protection primarily designed to mitigate?

options.text: A browser-based attacker causing an authenticated user's browser to submit unwanted state-changing requests
SQL injection in repository methods
Password brute force against a login endpoint
Cross-site scripting in static JavaScript files

questions.explanation: CSRF exploits the browser's automatic inclusion of credentials, such as cookies, in requests. CSRF tokens or suitable same-site and request design controls help mitigate it. Disabling CSRF requires understanding the application's authentication model and clients.

questions.question: For a stateless REST API authenticated with bearer tokens and not using browser cookies for authentication, what is a common CSRF configuration approach?

options.text: CSRF protection may be disabled for that API security chain after verifying the authentication and browser threat model
CSRF must always remain enabled for every endpoint
Replace bearer tokens with session cookies
Disable authorization checks

questions.explanation: CSRF risk is strongly tied to credentials automatically attached by browsers. A stateless bearer-token API that does not rely on ambient browser credentials often disables CSRF for that chain, but the decision must be based on the actual client and credential behavior.

questions.question: What is the purpose of method security such as `@PreAuthorize`?

options.text: To enforce authorization rules at method invocation boundaries
To configure database connection pooling
To serialize method return values
To enable component scanning

questions.explanation: Method security applies authorization expressions to method calls, enabling rules close to business operations rather than relying only on URL-level rules.

questions.question: In a JWT-based resource server, what should the API validate before trusting a token?

options.text: Signature and relevant claims such as issuer, audience, expiration, and allowed algorithms
Only the token's Base64-decoded payload
Only the username claim
Only that the token contains three dot-separated segments

questions.explanation: A JWT payload is not trustworthy merely because it can be decoded. Validate the signature using trusted keys and enforce relevant claims and algorithm policy, including issuer, audience, and expiration as required by the system.

questions.question: What is the role of an OAuth 2.0 resource server?

options.text: It protects resources by validating access tokens presented by clients
It issues database passwords to repositories
It replaces the identity provider in every deployment
It stores user interface preferences

questions.explanation: A resource server accepts requests with access tokens and validates them, then uses the resulting authentication and authorities to authorize access. Token issuance is typically performed by an authorization server.

questions.question: What does `hasRole("ADMIN")` commonly check in Spring Security?

options.text: For an authority named `ROLE_ADMIN` by default
For an authority named exactly `ADMIN` in every configuration
For a database column named ADMIN
For the user's OAuth client ID

questions.explanation: `hasRole("ADMIN")` conventionally applies the `ROLE_` prefix and checks for `ROLE_ADMIN`. `hasAuthority("ADMIN")` checks the exact authority string.

questions.question: Why should authorization be enforced in the service or method layer as well as, or instead of only, in the UI?

options.text: A client can bypass UI controls and call backend endpoints directly
The UI cannot display roles
Service methods cannot access the security context
Authorization in the backend slows all requests to zero

questions.explanation: UI controls improve usability but are not a security boundary. The server must enforce authorization on every protected operation because clients can be modified or bypassed.

questions.question: What does `@SpringBootTest` primarily do?

options.text: Loads a Spring application context for an integration-style test
Mocks every dependency automatically
Runs only repository tests
Starts a production deployment

questions.explanation: `@SpringBootTest` creates an application context using Boot's test support. It is useful for integration tests but can be slower than focused test slices or plain unit tests.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `@WebMvcTest`?

options.text: Loads a focused Spring MVC test slice, typically for controllers and related web components
Loads every production bean and external service
Starts a real production database by default
Tests only Java compiler behavior

questions.explanation: `@WebMvcTest` limits the context to MVC-related components. Collaborators such as services are commonly supplied as mocks, and requests can be exercised using MockMvc.

questions.question: What does `MockMvc` allow a test to do?

options.text: Exercise Spring MVC request handling without starting a real HTTP server
Run database migrations only
Mock JVM threads
Test a browser's CSS layout

questions.explanation: MockMvc performs requests through the Spring MVC infrastructure in-process, allowing assertions on status, headers, and response content without binding a network port.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `@DataJpaTest`?

options.text: Load a JPA-focused test slice for entity and repository behavior
Load all web and security components
Start a Kafka cluster automatically
Test only DTO validation

questions.explanation: `@DataJpaTest` configures a focused JPA test environment, scans entities and repositories, and commonly uses an embedded database when available unless configured otherwise.

questions.question: Why can an integration test pass with an embedded database but fail in production?

options.text: The embedded database may differ in SQL dialect, constraints, locking, and behavior from the production database
Embedded databases never support transactions
Spring Boot ignores JPA mappings in production
Production databases do not support indexes

questions.explanation: Database engines differ in SQL syntax, type handling, isolation, locking, constraints, and query planning. Testcontainers or a production-compatible database can expose these differences earlier.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `@MockBean` or its modern replacement patterns in Spring Boot tests?

options.text: To provide a mock in the Spring test application context in place of a bean
To create a mock HTTP server in every case
To generate a database schema
To bypass all test assertions

questions.explanation: Spring test bean-mocking support replaces or overrides a bean in the test context. In newer Spring Boot/Spring Framework versions, bean override and Mockito integration APIs may differ, so use the API supported by the project's version.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of Testcontainers for Spring Boot integration tests?

options.text: It runs dependencies such as databases in disposable containers, allowing tests against realistic services
It removes the need for assertions
It guarantees production data is copied into tests
It replaces the application context

questions.explanation: Testcontainers can provision disposable instances of real infrastructure such as PostgreSQL or Kafka. This improves fidelity compared with substitutes, while requiring container runtime support in the test environment.

questions.question: What does `@ActiveProfiles("test")` do in a Spring test?

options.text: Activates the named Spring profile for the test context
Changes the Java language version
Runs the test in a separate JVM automatically
Disables all auto-configuration

questions.explanation: `@ActiveProfiles` selects profile-specific configuration and beans for the test application context.

questions.question: Why should tests avoid depending on execution order or shared mutable database state?

options.text: Such dependencies make tests non-deterministic and can cause failures when tests run in parallel or isolation changes
JUnit requires tests to be order-independent only for performance
Database state is always reset automatically
Test order changes Java type inference

questions.explanation: Independent tests are easier to run repeatedly, in parallel, and in different environments. Use isolated fixtures, transactional rollback where appropriate, and explicit setup/cleanup.

questions.question: What is a good way to test a controller's validation behavior?

options.text: Send invalid request data through MockMvc and assert the expected status and error response
Call the controller method directly without validation infrastructure
Only test the DTO constructor
Inspect the source code manually

questions.explanation: An MVC-level test verifies request binding, Bean Validation, exception translation, and the resulting HTTP contract together.

questions.question: Which annotation is commonly used to declare a Spring-managed transaction boundary?

options.text: @Transactional
@RequestMapping
@Entity
@Async

questions.explanation: `@Transactional` typically applies transaction demarcation through Spring's transaction infrastructure, often using an AOP proxy around the method invocation.

questions.question: By default, which exception types cause Spring's declarative transaction to roll back?

options.text: RuntimeException and Error, but not checked exceptions by default
All checked and unchecked exceptions
Only SQLException
No exceptions cause rollback

questions.explanation: Spring's default rollback rules roll back on unchecked exceptions (`RuntimeException`) and `Error`. Checked exceptions do not trigger rollback by default unless rollback rules are configured.

questions.question: What does `Propagation.REQUIRED` mean?

options.text: Join the current transaction if one exists; otherwise create a new transaction
Always suspend the current transaction and create a new one
Never create or join a transaction
Run the method asynchronously

questions.explanation: `REQUIRED` is the default propagation behavior. It participates in an existing transaction or starts one when no transaction exists.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW`?

options.text: Suspend an existing transaction and execute within a new, independent transaction
Join the current transaction without changing it
Disable transaction synchronization
Retry the method after every exception

questions.explanation: `REQUIRES_NEW` suspends the current transaction, if present, and starts a new one. The inner transaction can commit or roll back independently of the outer transaction.

questions.question: Why might `@Transactional` appear not to work when one method in a class calls another annotated method on the same instance?

options.text: The self-invocation may bypass the Spring AOP proxy that applies transaction advice
Spring transactions only work on private fields
The database does not support transactions
The annotation is valid only on interfaces

questions.explanation: In the default proxy-based mode, calls must pass through the proxy for advice to run. A direct `this.someMethod()` call does not cross that proxy. Refactoring the transactional operation into another bean is often the cleanest fix.

questions.question: What does the READ COMMITTED isolation level generally prevent?

options.text: Dirty reads
All non-repeatable reads and phantom reads
All write skew anomalies
Every possible concurrency anomaly

questions.explanation: READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads. Non-repeatable reads and phantom reads may still occur, depending on the database implementation and transaction behavior.

questions.question: What is a likely trade-off of using SERIALIZABLE isolation?

options.text: Stronger isolation with potentially lower concurrency and more blocking or transaction retries
No locking or conflicts under any database
Guaranteed faster writes
Automatic distributed consistency across services

questions.explanation: Serializable isolation aims to make concurrent transactions behave as if executed serially. It can increase contention, blocking, aborts, and retry requirements.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `readOnly = true` on a transactional service method?

options.text: It communicates read-only intent and may allow transaction-provider or database optimizations; it is not a universal write-prevention guarantee
It encrypts all SELECT statements
It guarantees repeatable reads
It prevents the method from accessing repositories

questions.explanation: `readOnly` is a hint whose exact effect depends on the transaction manager and persistence provider. It should not be treated as a security boundary that universally prevents writes.

questions.question: What is the transactional outbox pattern intended to solve?

options.text: The dual-write problem when a service must update its database and publish an event reliably
The problem of choosing a database primary key
The need to validate JSON payloads
The problem of caching HTTP GET responses

questions.explanation: The service writes its business change and an outbox record in the same local database transaction. A separate publisher sends outbox events to the broker and marks them processed, enabling reliable eventual publication.

questions.question: What should a service typically do when a transaction fails due to a transient deadlock or serialization conflict?

options.text: Consider a bounded retry of the entire transaction where the operation is safe to retry
Ignore the exception and return success
Retry indefinitely inside the same failed transaction
Disable database constraints

questions.explanation: Transient concurrency failures can sometimes be retried, but the retry should wrap a fresh transaction, use a bounded policy with backoff, and account for idempotency and side effects.

questions.question: Which annotation is commonly used to enforce that a request field is not null during Bean Validation?

options.text: @NotNull
@Autowired
@Transactional
@Transient

questions.explanation: `@NotNull` is a Jakarta Bean Validation constraint. It is commonly applied to DTO fields and triggered when validation is requested, for example with `@Valid` on a controller parameter.

questions.question: What does `@Valid` on a `@RequestBody` parameter normally do?

options.text: Triggers validation of the deserialized object using its declared constraints
Encrypts the request body
Validates the caller's JWT signature
Starts a new transaction

questions.explanation: `@Valid` asks Spring MVC to validate the bound object. Constraint violations are typically translated into a validation exception that can be handled centrally.

questions.question: Which annotation is intended to handle exceptions across multiple controller classes?

options.text: @ControllerAdvice
@Service
@ConfigurationProperties
@EnableScheduling

questions.explanation: `@ControllerAdvice` provides cross-cutting controller functionality, including centralized exception handling with `@ExceptionHandler`. `@RestControllerAdvice` adds response-body semantics.

questions.question: What is a good API response practice for validation errors?

options.text: Return a stable error structure with field-level messages and an appropriate 4xx status
Return the complete Java stack trace to every client
Always return HTTP 200 with an error string
Return database credentials to help debugging

questions.explanation: Clients benefit from a predictable error contract containing an error code or message and field-level validation details. Internal stack traces and sensitive implementation details should remain in server logs.

questions.question: What is the difference between `@NotBlank` and `@NotEmpty` for a String?

options.text: @NotBlank rejects null, empty, and whitespace-only strings; @NotEmpty rejects null and empty but permits whitespace-only strings
They are identical
@NotEmpty rejects all strings longer than one character
@NotBlank only works on numeric fields

questions.explanation: `@NotBlank` requires at least one non-whitespace character. `@NotEmpty` requires a non-null value with nonzero length, so a string containing only spaces passes `@NotEmpty`.

questions.question: When using nested DTOs, what is commonly needed to cascade validation into a nested object?

options.text: Place `@Valid` on the nested property
Add `@Primary` to the nested property
Use `@Lazy` on the controller
Mark the nested object as `@Entity`

questions.explanation: Constraints on a nested object are not automatically traversed merely because the object is a field. `@Valid` on the nested property requests cascaded validation.

questions.question: Which exception is commonly raised by Spring MVC when request-body Bean Validation fails?

options.text: MethodArgumentNotValidException
NoSuchBeanDefinitionException
SQLException
ClassNotFoundException

questions.explanation: For many `@Valid @RequestBody` validation failures, Spring MVC raises `MethodArgumentNotValidException`. Method-level validation and newer framework versions can involve other exception types, so centralized handling should account for the application's actual validation path.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a domain-specific exception such as `OrderNotFoundException`?

options.text: To express a meaningful application failure that can be mapped consistently at the API boundary
To replace every checked and unchecked exception in Java
To make the database return HTTP status codes
To bypass transaction rollback rules

questions.explanation: Domain-specific exceptions communicate application meaning without coupling the domain layer to HTTP. The web layer can translate them into appropriate status codes and response bodies.

questions.question: Which HTTP status is generally appropriate when a client submits syntactically valid input that violates a business rule?

options.text: 400 Bad Request
101 Switching Protocols
301 Moved Permanently
503 Service Unavailable

questions.explanation: `400 Bad Request` is commonly used for invalid client input, including business-rule validation failures. Some APIs use `409 Conflict` for state conflicts; the important point is to define and apply a consistent contract.

questions.question: Why should an exception handler avoid returning raw exception messages from infrastructure libraries to clients?

options.text: They can reveal internal implementation details, sensitive data, or unstable messages not intended as an API contract
They prevent the JVM from collecting garbage
They always contain invalid Unicode
They cannot be serialized as JSON

questions.explanation: Raw infrastructure exception messages can expose SQL, hostnames, table names, or other internal details. Log diagnostic context securely and return a stable, sanitized API error.
